title: Semilinear invariance and computation of quadratic cotangent relations
statement: Let $(A,\mathfrak m)$ and $(A',\mathfrak m')$ be commutative local rings, with residue fields $k=A/\mathfrak m$ and $k'=A'/\mathfrak m'$, and finite dimensional cotangent spaces $V=\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$, $V'=\mathfrak m'/\mathfrak m'^2$. For a $k$-basis $x_1,\ldots,x_d$ of $V$, let $W_x$ be the $k$-vector space of homogeneous quadratic expressions $\sum_{i\le j}a_{ij}X_iX_j$, and define $\mu_x:W_x\to\mathfrak m^2/\mathfrak m^3$ by $X_iX_j\mapsto\widetilde x_i\widetilde x_j$; coefficients and basis elements may be lifted arbitrarily to $A$. Put $K_x=\ker\mu_x$. Define $K_{x'}$ in the same way for a basis of $V'$. Any ring isomorphism $\phi:A\cong A'$ induces a residue-field isomorphism $\sigma:k\cong k'$, a $\sigma$-semilinear cotangent bijection, and a $\sigma$-semilinear bijection $K_x\cong K_{x'}$ obtained by applying $\sigma$ to coefficients and substituting the images of the $X_i$. In dimension $d=2$, define the polar matrix of $aX_1^2+bX_1X_2+cX_2^2$ to be $B=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2a&b\\ b&2c\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ [def-weil-matrix, def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant]. If the linear substitution is written $X=P X'$ after applying $\sigma$, its polar matrix is $P^{\mathsf T}\sigma(B)P$, with determinant $(\det P)^2\sigma(\det B)$. Thus existence of a relation with invertible polar matrix is invariant under arbitrary ring isomorphisms, including in characteristic $2$. Furthermore, let $F$ be a field, $e\ge0$, $S=F[[z_1,\ldots,z_e]]$ [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series], $\mathfrak p=(z_1,\ldots,z_e)$ and $H\subseteq\mathfrak p^2$ an ideal. For $A=S/H$ the variable classes form an $F$-basis of $\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$ of dimension $e$. If $H=(f)$ and $f_2$ is the homogeneous degree-two part of $f$, then $K_z=F f_2$; this is zero when $f_2=0$. In particular for a nonzero homogeneous binary quadratic $Q$, the quadratic-relation space of $F[[u,v]]/(Q)$ is the one-dimensional span of $Q$.

proof.text: First the map $\mu_x$ is well defined and $k$-linear. Replacing a lift $\widetilde x_i$ by $\widetilde x_i+t$ with $t\in\mathfrak m^2$ changes a product by an element of $\mathfrak m^3$. Replacing a coefficient lift by an element differing by $s\in\mathfrak m$ changes its product with two basis lifts by an element of $\mathfrak m^3$. Since $\mathfrak m(\mathfrak m^2/\mathfrak m^3)=0$, scalar multiplication on this quotient factors through $k$; addition and scalar multiplication of the displayed expressions therefore give a $k$-linear map. This uses no choice of a coefficient field in $A$.

source.place: Tag 0C49, lemma-nodal-algebraic, preceding definition and conditions (1)--(3); agent-written details of the intrinsic quadratic relation calculation.

proof.text: A ring isomorphism preserves units and nonunits. In a local ring the nonunits are precisely its maximal ideal, hence $\phi(\mathfrak m)=\mathfrak m\prime$. Applying $\phi$ to finite sums of products gives $\phi(\mathfrak m^r)=\mathfrak m\prime{}^r$ for $r=2,3$, with the reverse inclusion from $\phi^{-1}$. Thus $[a]\mapsto[\phi(a)]$ gives the residue-field isomorphism $\sigma$ and the additive bijections $V\to V\prime$ and $\mathfrak m^2/\mathfrak m^3\to\mathfrak m\prime{}^2/\mathfrak m\prime{}^3$. The identity $\phi(ab)=\phi(a)\phi(b)$ proves their $\sigma$-semilinearity.

source.place: Tag 0C49, lemma-nodal-algebraic, preceding definition and conditions (1)--(3); agent-written details of the intrinsic quadratic relation calculation.

proof.text: Express the image of each $x_i$ in the basis $x\prime_j$, and define $T:W_x\to W_{x\prime}$ by applying $\sigma$ to coefficients and replacing $X_i$ by that linear expression in $X\prime_j$. Products of two basis lifts show term by term that $\mu_{x\prime}T=\phi_2\mu_x$, where $\phi_2$ is the degree-two quotient bijection from step 2; errors in the chosen linear lifts lie in $\mathfrak m\prime{}^2$ and hence disappear after multiplication modulo $\mathfrak m\prime{}^3$. Substitution associated to $\phi^{-1}$ is inverse to $T$, since their composites fix coefficients and each variable. Consequently $T$ restricts to a $\sigma$-semilinear bijection of the two kernels.

source.place: Tag 0C49, lemma-nodal-algebraic, preceding definition and conditions (1)--(3); agent-written details of the intrinsic quadratic relation calculation.

proof.text: For the binary calculation put $A_0=\sigma(a)$, $B_0=\sigma(b)$, $C_0=\sigma(c)$ and write $P_{11}=p$, $P_{12}=q$, $P_{21}=r$, $P_{22}=s$. Under $X_1=pX\prime_1+qX\prime_2$, $X_2=rX\prime_1+sX\prime_2$ the coefficients become $a\prime=A_0p^2+B_0pr+C_0r^2$, $b\prime=2A_0pq+B_0(ps+qr)+2C_0rs$, $c\prime=A_0q^2+B_0qs+C_0s^2$. Multiplying entries gives $B\prime=P^{\mathsf T}\sigma(B)P$, where $B\prime_{11}=2a\prime$, $B\prime_{12}=B\prime_{21}=b\prime$, $B\prime_{22}=2c\prime$. The two-term determinant formula and expansion give $4a\prime c\prime-(b\prime)^2=(ps-qr)^2\sigma(4ac-b^2)$.

source.place: Tag 0C49, lemma-nodal-algebraic, preceding definition and conditions (1)--(3); agent-written details of the intrinsic quadratic relation calculation.

proof.text: The inverse substitution in step 3 gives an inverse matrix for $P$, so $ps-qr$ is a nonzero element of $k\prime$. The determinant identity in step 4 therefore preserves nonvanishing in both directions. For a $2\times2$ matrix over a field, a nonzero determinant gives its inverse by the explicit adjugate formula; conversely a nonzero kernel vector when the determinant is zero prevents invertibility. Hence a relation has invertible polar matrix if and only if its transported relation does. No division by $2$ occurred: in characteristic $2$ the determinant is $-b^2$ and the same formulas apply.

source.place: Tag 0C49, lemma-nodal-algebraic, preceding definition and conditions (1)--(3); agent-written details of the intrinsic quadratic relation calculation.

proof.text: Apply the coefficient criterion with coefficient ring $F$, coefficient ideal $J=0$, $d=e$, and $n=1,2,3$. It says that a series lies in $\mathfrak p^n$ exactly when its coefficients of total degree $<n$ vanish. Thus the degree-$n$ monomials give an $F$-basis of $\mathfrak p^n/\mathfrak p^{n+1}$ for $n=1,2$: subtract the finite homogeneous degree-$n$ part for spanning, and read its coefficients for independence. Multiplication of these representatives is the finite coefficient-convolution product of formal series.

source.place: Tag 032C, remark-Noetherian-complete-local-ring-universally-catenary, motivating power-series local rings; existing combined-ideal coefficient lemma supplies the stronger explicit criterion.

proof.text: By the power-series locality lemma, $S$ is local and its maximal ideal consists of the series with zero constant coefficient. Step 6 identifies it with $\mathfrak p$. Since $H\subseteq\mathfrak p^2\subseteq\mathfrak p$, the proper quotient $A=S/H$ is local with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m=\mathfrak p/H$: elements outside it lift to units, and its quotient is $F$. Products of lifts give $\mathfrak m^n=(\mathfrak p^n+H)/H$. The map $\mathfrak p/\mathfrak p^2\to\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$ is bijective: it is surjective and its kernel is $(\mathfrak p^2+H)/\mathfrak p^2=0$. Step 6 gives the claimed variable basis of dimension $e$.

source.place: Tag 032C, remark-Noetherian-complete-local-ring-universally-catenary, motivating power-series local rings; existing combined-ideal coefficient lemma supplies the stronger explicit criterion.

proof.text: Using step 6 to identify $W_z$ with $\mathfrak p^2/\mathfrak p^3$, its multiplication map for $A$ is the map to $(\mathfrak p^2+H)/(\mathfrak p^3+H)$. A homogeneous quadratic polynomial $q$ belongs to its kernel exactly when $q\in\mathfrak p^3+H$. If $H=(f)$, write $q=t+gf$ with $t\in\mathfrak p^3$, $g\in S$. The Cauchy coefficient formula, and the vanishing of the degree-zero and degree-one coefficients of $f\in\mathfrak p^2$, give $(gf)_2=g(0)f_2$, hence $q=g(0)f_2$. Conversely $\lambda f-\lambda f_2\in\mathfrak p^3$ for each $\lambda\in F$, so every $\lambda f_2$ belongs to the kernel. This proves $K_z=Ff_2$.

source.place: Tag 0C49, lemma-nodal-algebraic, preceding definition and conditions (1)--(3); agent-written details of the intrinsic quadratic relation calculation.

proof.text: If $f_2=0$, its span is zero. For $e=0$, $S=F$ and $\mathfrak p=0$, so $H=0$, the variable basis is empty and the same calculation gives the zero relation space. Finally when $e=2$ and $f=Q$ is nonzero homogeneous quadratic, $f_2=Q$; comparison of a nonzero coefficient makes $\lambda\mapsto\lambda Q$ injective, so $FQ$ is one dimensional. This proves the last assertion without any nondegeneracy assumption on $Q$.
